page_title: Graph Types and Representations
summary: This lecture page introduces fundamental graph theory concepts essential for Deep Graph Learning, categorizing graphs by their structural properties such as directionality, weighting, and connectivity. It defines specific graph classes including simple, complete, hyper, heterogeneous, and annotated graphs, providing formal definitions and visual examples for each. The content concludes by detailing how graphs are mathematically represented using adjacency, feature, and edge matrices to facilitate computational processing.
key_topics: graph taxonomy|graph representation|matrix encoding|graph properties

page_title: Graph Properties and Matrix Representations
summary: This lecture page introduces fundamental graph properties including connectivity, scale, and permutation invariance, alongside matrix representations like adjacency matrices. It covers topological concepts such as efficiency, resilience, and centrality measures, while exploring spectral properties through eigen decomposition and matrix powers for analyzing graph walks.
key_topics: adjacency matrix|graph topology|permutation invariance|eigen decomposition|graph walks|centrality measures

page_title: Graph Neural Network Prediction Tasks
summary: This page details three primary prediction tasks in Deep Graph Learning: graph classification, node classification, and edge prediction. It illustrates how Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) generate node embeddings which are then processed via pooling or dot products to produce outputs for these tasks. The page also provides the mathematical definitions for the logistic activation (sigmoid) function and its derivative, which are used to map network outputs to probabilities.
key_topics: graph classification|node classification|edge prediction|node embedding|logistic activation

page_title: Deep Learning Preliminaries: Regression, Networks, and Representation Learning
summary: This lecture page reviews supervised regression models, contrasting single and multi-output linear approaches with their corresponding neural network architectures. It introduces the transition from hand-crafted features to learnable representations via matrix factorization techniques like PCA and K-Means. Finally, it outlines the structure of deep nonlinear networks, emphasizing composition, activation functions, and backpropagation.
key_topics: supervised regression|neural network architecture|matrix factorization|representation learning|deep learning

page_title: Feature Embedding and Graph-Based Learning
summary: This lecture page contrasts traditional machine learning formalization, where data points are treated as independent samples on a high-dimensional manifold, with graph-based learning approaches that model interactions between data points. It introduces manifold learning concepts including intrinsic and extrinsic dimensions, and explains how graph neural networks can extract node-based, edge-based, and graph-based features to capture relationships in data.
key_topics: manifold learning|feature embedding|graph neural networks|dimensionality reduction|graph-based features

page_title: Graph Neural Networks and Node Embedding
summary: This lecture page contrasts classical node embedding with Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), emphasizing the shift from individualistic to collectivist learning paradigms. It details the GCN layer-wise propagation rule, including self-loop augmentation and normalization to manage gradient stability. The content also covers the mathematical foundations of node similarity, receptive fields via graph walks, and the architecture of deep sequential representation learning.
key_topics: graph convolutional network|node embedding|message passing|graph adjacency matrix|receptive field|layer-wise normalization

page_title: Graph Convolutional Network Layer Mechanics and Graph Classification
summary: This page details the mathematical formulation of Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) layers, specifically focusing on the update rules for node embeddings through neighborhood aggregation and linear transformation. It contrasts the 'vanilla' GCN approach with enhanced versions that include learnable self-loops or separate self-transformation weights. The lecture concludes by demonstrating how these sequential layers are utilized for graph-level tasks, such as graph classification, using a readout function and an MLP classifier.
key_topics: graph convolutional network|message passing|node embedding|graph classification|self-loop augmentation

page_title: GCN Training and Optimization Pipeline
summary: This page details the training process for Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), focusing on the message passing mechanism, loss function optimization via gradient descent, and the distinction between transductive and inductive learning. It outlines the mathematical formulation for updating node embeddings through neighborhood aggregation and linear transformation, and defines the prediction heads for node and edge classification tasks.

page_title: Graph-Level Prediction and Inductive Capability of GCNs
summary: This lecture page explores the inductive capability of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), focusing on their ability to generalize to new nodes and graphs of varying sizes. It details methods for graph-level prediction, specifically how to combine node embeddings into a single graph representation using global pooling techniques like mean, max, and sum. The content also introduces hierarchical pooling (DiffPool) as a method to better differentiate graph structures and discusses the importance of parameter sharing for efficient learning across different graph topologies.

page_title: GNN Layer Operations and Architecture

page_title: Graph Neural Network Aggregation and Attention Mechanisms
summary: This page details the core operations of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), focusing on local and global aggregation strategies. It contrasts standard Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) using Kipf normalization with Graph Attention Networks (GATs) that utilize learnable attention weights. The content covers specific mathematical formulations for message passing, including mean aggregation, max pooling, and the integration of softmax-normalized attention masks.

page_title: GNN Training Strategies and Batching
summary: This lecture page details the computational challenges of training Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), specifically the graph expansion problem where receptive fields grow exponentially with depth. It compares three optimization strategies: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), Batch Gradient Descent, and Mini-batch Gradient Descent, highlighting the trade-offs in memory usage, convergence stability, and computational efficiency. The page introduces GraphSAGE as a solution for scalable training through random neighborhood sampling and discusses graph partitioning as an alternative batching method.
key_topics: graph expansion problem|mini-batch gradient descent|graphsage|receptive field|node embedding computation graph|graph partitioning

page_title: GNN Training: Sampling Strategies and Batch Normalization
summary: This lecture page details methods to improve the computational efficiency and stability of training Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) on large graphs. It contrasts three primary sampling strategies—node-wise (GraphSAGE), layer-wise (FastGCN), and subgraph-based (ClusterGCN, GraphSAINT)—highlighting their trade-offs regarding memory usage, redundancy, and structural preservation. Additionally, it explains the role of Batch Normalization (BN) in stabilizing forward propagation, controlling covariate shift, and enabling higher learning rates through regularization.
key_topics: graph neural network training|sampling strategies|batch normalization|computational efficiency|covariate shift

page_title: GNN Layer Architecture and Dropout Regularization
summary: This page details the components of a single Graph Neural Network (GNN) layer, including transformation, aggregation, and normalization steps. page_title: Inductive vs. Transductive Learning and Graph Classification
summary: This page contrasts inductive and transductive learning paradigms in graph neural networks, highlighting differences in training data access, memory usage, and generalization capabilities. It details the architecture for graph classification, involving node embeddings, global pooling, and a sigmoid activation for output prediction. Formulas for both graph-level and node-level classification are presented, emphasizing the role of learned weights and bias terms.
key_topics: inductive learning|transductive learning|graph classification|node classification|global pooling|graph neural network

page_title: Permutation Invariance and Equivariance in Graph Neural Networks
summary: This lecture page defines and contrasts permutation invariance and equivariance within the context of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). It establishes that GNNs must be permutation invariant for graph-level tasks (like classification) so that the output does not depend on node indexing, while node-level tasks require permutation equivariance where embeddings permute consistently with the input. The content includes mathematical formalizations using permutation matrices to demonstrate how adjacency and feature matrices transform under reordering.
key_topics: permutation invariance|permutation equivariance|graph neural networks|permutation matrices|graph classification

page_title: Expressive Power of Graph Neural Networks and the Weisfeiler-Lehman Test
summary: This lecture page explores the theoretical limits of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in distinguishing graph structures, defining expressive power as the ability to map distinct local neighborhoods to unique embeddings. It introduces the Graph Isomorphism Network (GIN) as a model designed to achieve maximum expressiveness by utilizing injective aggregation functions, mathematically equivalent to the Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) graph isomorphism test. The content contrasts standard aggregators like mean and max, which fail to distinguish certain non-isomorphic graphs, with the WL color refinement algorithm that iteratively hashes neighborhood structures to differentiate nodes.
key_topics: expressive power of gnn|weisfeiler-lehman graph isomorphism test|injective aggregation|graph isomorphism network|node computational graph

page_title: Graph Isomorphism Network (GIN) and Expressiveness
summary: This page details the Graph Isomorphism Network (GIN), a maximally expressive GNN architecture that matches the power of the Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) test. It presents the theoretical conditions for GNN expressiveness, specifically requiring injective aggregation functions, and contrasts GIN with less expressive models like GCN and GraphSAGE. The page includes the specific GIN message update rule and architectural diagrams illustrating pre-layers, GNN layers, and post-layers for node and graph classification tasks.
key_topics: graph isomorphism network|weisfeiler-lehman test|gnn expressiveness|injective aggregation|message passing

page_title: Encoder-Decoder GNNs and Graph Generation
